blocks.title: Definitions
blocks.content:
Definitions
The definitions below apply to terms as used in these guidelines, and they may have different 
meanings elsewhere.
Active (tuberculosis) case-finding (ACF): Provider-initiated screening and testing in communities 
by mobile teams, often using mobile X-ray and rapid molecular tests. The term is sometimes used 
synonymously with “systematic screening”.
Computer-aided detection (CAD): The use of specialized software to interpret abnormalities on 
chest radiographs that are suggestive of TB. The results are expressed as abnormality scores. CAD 
may be used for screening or triage.
Enha

summary.text: Defines the key terms used in the TB screening guidelines, including active, enhanced and passive case-finding, computer-aided detection, number needed to screen and repeat screening. It also explains initial screening, triage and the meaning of TB disease as distinct from TB infection.

blocks.title: Executive summary
blocks.content:
Executive summary
Tuberculosis (TB) is a leading cause of death from a single infectious agent, despite being largely 
curable and preventable. In 2019 an estimated 2.9 million of the 10 million people who fell ill with TB 
were not diagnosed or reported to the World Health Organization (WHO). The Political Declaration 
adopted by the United Nations General Assembly in September 2018 at the High-Level Meeting on 
the Fight Against Tuberculosis commits to, among other goals, diagnosing and treating 40 million 
people with TB by 2022. In order to achieve this ambitious target, there is an urgent

summary.text: Summarizes why WHO updated its 2013 guidance on systematic TB screening, citing the 2.9 million people with TB who went undiagnosed or unreported in 2019 and global targets for diagnosis. It explains that a Guideline Development Group reviewed new evidence in 2020, including on computer-aided detection of chest X-rays, C-reactive protein and rapid molecular tests. The summary presents the recommendations on which populations to screen and which tools to use, ending with a box on the main changes from the earlier guidance.

blocks.title: Background
blocks.content:
Tuberculosis (TB) is a leading cause of death from a single infectious agent, despite being largely 
curable and preventable. In 2019, an estimated 2.9 million of the 10 million people who fell ill with TB 
were not diagnosed or reported to the World Health Organization (WHO) (1). WHO’s End TB Strategy 
envisions a 90% reduction in TB incidence and a 95% reduction in TB deaths by 2035 (2, 3), and the 
Declaration adopted by the United Nations General Assembly in September 2018 at the High-Level 
Meeting on the Fight Against Tuberculosis commits to diagnosing and treating 40 million people 
wit

summary.text: Gives the background to the update, noting the gap in TB diagnosis, the End TB Strategy and UN targets, and the new evidence on screening since WHO's 2013 guidelines.

blocks.title: Definition and objectives of systematic screening for TB disease
blocks.content:
for TB disease
For the purpose of this guideline, systematic screening for TB disease is defined as the systematic 
identification of people at risk for TB disease, in a predetermined target group, by assessing 
symptoms and using tests, examinations or other procedures that can be applied rapidly. 
The screening tests, examinations and other procedures should efficiently distinguish people with a 
high probability of having TB disease from those who are unlikely to have TB disease. Among those 
whose screening is positive, the diagnosis needs to be established by diagnostic evaluation, consis

summary.text: Defines systematic screening for TB disease as provider-initiated identification of people at risk in a target group using rapid tests, followed by diagnostic confirmation. It sets out the two aims of screening: early detection and treatment for individuals, and reduced transmission and incidence in the population.

summary.text: Presents the conceptual framework for the 2021 update, linking screening inputs and activities to individual and population outcomes such as earlier diagnosis, better treatment results and reduced transmission. It then lists the PICO and background questions used to gather evidence, covering effectiveness, screening tool accuracy, numbers needed to screen, risk factors, costs and community attitudes.

blocks.title: Rationale for the guideline update
blocks.content:
Since the publication of the first WHO guidelines on systematic screening for TB in 2013 (5), there 
have been numerous studies, including reviews, randomized controlled trials, observational studies, 
modelling and cost–effectiveness research, evaluating the real or potential impacts of screening 
interventions on both individual-level and community-level outcomes related to TB. There have also 
been numerous prevalence surveys since 2013, which have shed new light on the magnitude of the 
burden of TB in several key countries. The majority of prevalence surveys have shown that the burden 
of

summary.text: Explains that the update was prompted by many new studies on screening impact and by prevalence surveys showing a larger TB burden than previously thought.

blocks.title: Objectives of guideline update
blocks.content:
The specific objectives of the guideline update are:
1.	 to support Member States in implementing effective TB screening interventions by providing 
updated information about the expected impact of TB screening on patient-important outcomes 
and the epidemiology of TB, the expected yield of screening interventions and the expected 
performance of different screening tools and algorithms;
2.	 to contribute to finding more people with TB and finding them earlier in the course of disease 
in order to reduce disease burden, morbidity and mortality, and costs and financial hardship for 
people suff

summary.text: States the objectives of the update: to help countries implement effective screening with current evidence on impact, yield and tool performance, and to find more people with TB earlier.

blocks.title: Target audience
blocks.content:
This guideline is intended for personnel working in national TB programmes, national HIV/AIDS 
programmes or their equivalents, and other relevant national health programmes in ministries 
of health; other relevant ministries working in public health and screening; and for other health 
policymakers, clinicians and public health practitioners working on TB, HIV and infectious diseases in 
the public and private sectors. The recommendations provided here must be adapted to local settings. 
An accompanying operational handbook, WHO operational handbook on tuberculosis. Module 2: 
screening – sys

summary.text: Identifies the intended readers of the guideline, such as national TB and HIV programme staff, policymakers and clinicians, and points to an accompanying operational handbook for adapting the recommendations locally.

blocks.title: Recommendations for systematic screening for TB disease in targeted populations
blocks.content:
systematic screening for TB 
disease in targeted populations
In this guideline, recommendations about systematic screening for TB disease are made for distinct 
populations for whom it is judged that the benefits and desirable effects of screening outweigh the 
potential harms. 
Systematic screening for TB disease can be done for an entire population (community-wide screening) 
or it can be targeted at selected risk groups or subpopulations of people who may be at higher risk of 
being exposed to TB, developing TB disease or suffering poor outcomes from the disease, or some 
combination of the

summary.text: Introduces the population-specific recommendations, explaining that screening may cover whole communities or be targeted at higher-risk groups and how strong and conditional recommendations are distinguished. It sets out the recommendation on screening the general population in high-prevalence settings. The evidence reviewed includes trials and studies in which community-wide screening reduced TB prevalence or infection among children.

blocks.title: Systematic screening for TB disease in the general population
blocks.content:

defined as a 1% prevalence or higher. Based on the updated evidence reviewed, the GDG concluded 
that the threshold of 1% recommended in the 2013 guidelines could be lowered, but considered 
that screening under programmatic conditions would not perform as well as was observed in the 
trial in Viet Nam and, therefore, proposed a 0.5% threshold to guide country implementation. Thus, 
the GDG recommended that general population screening may be considered in defined areas 
with a prevalence of undetec

summary.text: Explains why the prevalence threshold for general population screening was lowered from 1% to 0.5% undetected TB, and discusses implementation factors such as prevalence, coverage and the sensitivity of screening algorithms. It also covers possible harms and concerns of people being screened, such as stigma and confidentiality.

blocks.title: Systematic screening for TB disease among people with structural risk factors for TB
blocks.content:
people with structural risk factors for TB
2. Systematic screening for TB disease may be conducted among subpopulations with structural 
risk factors for TB. These include urban poor communities, homeless communities, communities 
in remote or isolated areas, indigenous populations, migrants, refugees, internally displaced 
persons and other vulnerable or marginalized groups with limited access to health care 
(existing recommendation: conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence).
2.2.1 Summary of evidence and rationale
Populations with structural risk factors for TB are those t

summary.text: Gives the conditional recommendation to screen groups with structural risk factors, such as urban poor, homeless, remote, indigenous, migrant and displaced populations, and explains these risk factors. It notes that no new evidence was found since 2013 and offers implementation advice, including combining TB screening with other health activities.

blocks.title: Systematic screening for TB disease among people living with HIV
blocks.content:
people living with HIV
3. People living with HIV should be systematically screened for TB disease at each visit to a 
health facility 
(existing recommendation: strong recommendation, very low certainty of evidence).
2.3.1 Summary of evidence and rationale
People living with HIV are approximately 19 times more likely to develop TB disease than those without 
HIV; in 2019, an estimated 44% of people living with HIV who also had TB disease did not reach care, 
and 30% of all HIV-related deaths were due to TB (1). Thus, ensuring early detection and treatment 
for TB among all people living with H

summary.text: Sets out the strong recommendation that people living with HIV be screened for TB at every health facility visit, citing their much higher TB risk, and describes follow-up diagnostic testing and preventive treatment.

blocks.title: Systematic screening for TB disease among household and other close contacts of individuals with TB disease
blocks.content:
household and other close contacts of individuals 
with TB disease 
4. Household contacts and other close contacts of individuals with TB disease should be 
systematically screened for TB disease 
(updated recommendation: strong recommendation, moderate certainty of evidence).
2.4.1 Summary of evidence and rationale
Household and close contacts of individuals with TB disease are at high risk of TB infection and 
developing TB disease. A systematic review conducted for the guideline update found the weighted 
pooled prevalence of TB disease among all close contacts of TB patients was 3.6% (95%

summary.text: Gives the updated strong recommendation to screen household and close contacts of people with TB, citing a pooled disease prevalence of 3.6% and trials in Viet Nam, South Africa and Zambia showing benefits. It then covers implementation, including prioritizing contacts and offering HIV testing and preventive treatment where appropriate.

blocks.title: Systematic screening for TB disease in prisons and other penitentiary institutions
blocks.content:
and other penitentiary institutions
5. Systematic screening for TB disease should be conducted in prisons and penitentiary 
institutions 
(updated recommendation: strong recommendation, very low certainty of evidence).
2.5.1 Summary of evidence and rationale
People in prisons and other penitentiary institutions are at an increased risk for TB compared with 
the general population, and they often have limited access to health care services. The estimated 
incidence of TB among people residing in prisons is 23 times higher than that among the general 
population (24). Data reviewed for the GDG m

summary.text: Presents the updated strong recommendation for TB screening in prisons, citing a much higher TB incidence among prisoners and studies showing earlier and increased case detection. Implementation advice covers screening at entry and periodically, infection control and access to diagnosis.

blocks.title: Systematic screening for TB disease among miners and others exposed to silica dust
blocks.content:
miners and others exposed to silica dust 
6. Current and former workers in workplaces with silica exposure should be systematically 
screened for TB disease 
(existing recommendation: strong recommendation, low certainty of evidence).
2.6.1 Summary of evidence and rationale
Exposure to silica dust and silicosis are among the strongest risk factors for TB, with a relative risk of 
2.8–39 for silicosis, depending on the severity of the disease (30). Silicosis is common in miners (31, 32), 
which is a primary reason for the high incidence of TB among them, and this is often compounded 
by a high

summary.text: Sets out the strong recommendation to screen current and former workers exposed to silica dust, given the high TB risk linked to silicosis, and advises screening at least every 12 months, ideally combined with improvements to working conditions.

blocks.title: Systematic screening for TB disease among people attending health care services who have clinical risk factors for TB
blocks.content:
people attending health care services who have 
clinical risk factors for TB
7. In settings where the TB prevalence in the general population is 100/100 000 population or 
higher, systematic screening for TB disease may be conducted among people with a risk factor 
for TB who are either seeking health care or who are already in care 
(existing recommendation: conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence).
8. People with an untreated fibrotic lesion seen on chest X-ray may be systematically screened 
for TB disease 
(existing recommendation: conditional recommendation, very low ce

summary.text: Gives conditional recommendations to screen people with clinical TB risk factors in health care settings where prevalence is at least 100 per 100,000, and people with untreated fibrotic lesions on chest X-ray. It reviews evidence on risk factors such as HIV, diabetes, malnutrition, smoking and alcohol use, summarized in a table. Implementation points include prioritizing groups according to local epidemiology, offering preventive treatment where appropriate and considering screening of health care workers.

blocks.title: Recommendations for tools for systematic screening for TB disease
blocks.content:
for systematic screening for TB 
disease
TB screening tools are designed to distinguish people with a higher probability of having TB disease 
from those with a low probability and can be assumed to be free of TB disease. They are not intended 
to provide a definitive diagnosis. In general, they need to be able to be implemented easily and relay 
results rapidly in order to be informative in a screening context. Screening tests need to be followed 
by a diagnostic test, offered as part of a comprehensive clinical evaluation, to confirm or rule out TB 
disease in individuals who screen positive

summary.text: Introduces the recommendations on screening tools, explaining that tools separate people likely to have TB from those unlikely to have it and must be followed by diagnostic tests, and cites WHO target accuracy benchmarks.

blocks.title: Tools for screening for TB disease among the general population and high-risk groups
blocks.content:
general population and high-risk groups 
9. Among individuals aged 15 years and older in populations in which TB screening is 
recommended, systematic screening for TB disease may be conducted using a symptom screen, 
chest X-ray or molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests, alone or in combination 
(new recommendation: conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence for 
test accuracy).
3.1.1 Summary of the evidence and rationale
The data used to inform this recommendation came from a systematic review of the diagnostic 
accuracy of using symptoms and chest radiography to de

summary.text: Recommends that people aged 15 and over in groups eligible for screening may be screened with symptom questions, chest X-ray or rapid molecular tests, alone or combined. It summarizes systematic review evidence on the accuracy of each tool, with a table of sensitivity and specificity. The section closes by advising countries to fit these tools into national algorithms according to goals, resources and equity.

blocks.title: Use of computer-aided detection software for automated reading of digital chest radiographs
blocks.content:
automated reading of digital chest radiographs
10. Among individuals aged 15 years and older in populations in which TB screening is 
recommended, computer-aided detection software programmes may be used in place of 
human readers for interpreting digital chest X-rays for screening and triage for TB disease 
(new recommendation: conditional recommendation, low certainty of evidence).
3.2.1 Summary of the evidence and rationale
The use of CXR to screen for TB is a practice that goes back several decades. CXRs are also routinely 
used for triage of patients presenting to care who are displaying

summary.text: Presents a new conditional recommendation that computer-aided detection software may replace human readers in interpreting digital chest X-rays for TB screening and triage in people aged 15 and over. It explains that chest radiography is limited by shortages of trained readers and variability between readers, and that many software packages now estimate the likelihood of TB. It ends with implementation needs such as digital radiography equipment, stable internet and maintenance, noting that costs depend on the setting.

blocks.title: Tools for screening for TB disease among people living with HIV
blocks.content:
living with HIV
11. Among adults and adolescents living with HIV, systematic screening for TB disease should 
be conducted using the WHO-recommended four symptom screen and those who report any 
one of the symptoms of current cough, fever, weight loss or night sweats may have TB and 
should be evaluated for TB and other diseases 
(existing recommendation: strong recommendation, moderate certainty of evidence).
12. Among adults and adolescents living with HIV, C-reactive protein with a cut-off of > 5 mg/L 
may be used to screen for TB disease 
(new recommendation: conditional recommendation, lo

summary.text: Sets out recommendations on tools for TB screening among adults and adolescents living with HIV, keeping the four-symptom screen and adding C-reactive protein above 5 mg/L, chest X-ray and molecular rapid tests as options. It also strongly recommends systematic molecular testing of HIV inpatients in medical wards where TB prevalence exceeds 10%. The section summarises the evidence on the accuracy of these tools, as the start and end of this cut block show. It ends by encouraging countries to monitor screening yield among people with HIV by screening tool.

blocks.title: Tools for systematic screening for TB disease among children and adolescents
blocks.content:
among children and adolescents 
16. Among individuals younger than 15 years who are close contacts of someone with TB, 
systematic screening for TB disease should be conducted using a symptom screen including 
any one of cough, fever or poor weight gain; or chest radiography; or both 
(new recommendation: strong recommendation, moderate to low certainty of evidence for test 
accuracy). 
17. Among children younger than 10 years who are living with HIV, systematic screening for 
TB disease should be conducted using a symptom screen including any one of current cough, 
fever, poor weight gain or

summary.text: Gives recommendations for screening children and adolescents, using symptoms, chest radiography or both for close contacts under 15, and a symptom screen including contact history for children under 10 with HIV. It notes that children accounted for about 12% of TB cases but 16% of deaths in 2019, showing the need for better case detection. It advises placing these tools within national screening and diagnostic algorithms described in the operational handbook.

blocks.title: Monitoring and evaluation
blocks.content:
4. Monitoring and evaluation
In this section, we consider the monitoring and evaluation required to support the implementation of 
TB screening programmes. The operational handbook contains more details about the monitoring, 
surveillance and evaluation of TB screening interventions (7).
When considering implementing screening in the general population, it is important to know the 
epidemiology of TB and the prevalence of undetected TB in the community. This will help to estimate 
the impact of any screening programme. TB disease prevalence surveys are used to assess the 
baseline occurrence o

summary.text: Explains that planning TB screening requires knowing local TB epidemiology, using prevalence surveys or notification data alongside risk factors. It advises monitoring in high-burden settings such as prisons and allows screening to stop when the burden stays low, with surveillance continuing.

blocks.title: Indicators

summary.text: Lists indicators for monitoring TB screening in each risk group, from numbers eligible and screened to diagnoses, number needed to screen, initial defaulters and treatment outcomes. It notes the value of disaggregation and the difficulty of estimating eligible populations in community outreach.

blocks.title: Routines for recording and reporting
blocks.content:
In order to obtain the required information for the indicators described above, a TB recording and 
reporting system needs to include a minimal set of data elements. Although paper-based systems have 
been used to collect such data, it is now becoming increasingly feasible to collect data electronically, 
and this should be the standard aspired to for monitoring TB screening activities. The following 
strategies can be used to collect the necessary data:
•	 maintain a log of the number of people screened in each risk group. A special register with 
individual-level information for each person

summary.text: Describes the minimum recording and reporting needed for TB screening indicators, preferably electronic, including logs of people screened and registers of people with presumptive TB. It recommends adding fields to laboratory and treatment registers showing whether patients were found through screening and their risk group.

blocks.title: Programmatic evaluations
blocks.content:
A successful screening programme may lead to a diminishing yield, at least if the risk group is a fixed 
population. Over time, changes in the background burden of TB, as well as changes in the profile 
of TB patients in the community (e.g. a trend towards fewer patients with symptomatic TB) can lead 
to a reduction in the yield from screening, an increase in the NNS, a reduction in cost–effectiveness 
and a change in the ratio of benefits to harms. Trends in all of these indicators need to be monitored, 
and the prioritization of risk groups, choice of screening approach and screening interva

summary.text: Explains that screening yield may fall over time, so indicators and choices of risk groups, approaches and intervals should be reassessed, with stopping criteria set in advance. It notes that unexpected indicator results may call for special assessments of barriers to screening.

blocks.title: Initial calibration for computer-aided detection technologies
blocks.content:
technologies
When CAD is implemented, local calibration is advised to customize the score thresholds to the 
requirements of the programme (see the operational handbook for more details about how this can 
be done) (7). After this initial calibration, ongoing monitoring and analysis of CAD performance should 
be carried out to assess the correlation with human readers’ interpretations and with bacteriological 
confirmation, and with the proportion of images read as abnormal and requiring further investigation.

summary.text: Advises local calibration of computer-aided detection score thresholds and ongoing monitoring of its performance against human readers and bacteriological results.

blocks.title: Research gaps
blocks.content: 5. Research gaps

summary.text: A section heading for the chapter on research gaps.

blocks.title: Screening for TB in targeted populations
blocks.content:
5.1.1 The general population and high-risk groups
Well-designed trials and rigorous quasi-experimental studies in different settings are required to 
investigate the effects of population-wide systematic screening for TB on individual-level outcomes 
(diagnostic delay, treatment outcomes, costs to patients, social consequences) and population-
level outcomes (TB prevalence, incidence, transmission), as well as to guide implementation choices 
(including the method of delivery, screening algorithms, the duration of screening intervals and 
frequency of screening, and the mode of delivering the

summary.text: Identifies research needs on population-wide and targeted TB screening, including trials of effects on individual and population outcomes, implementation choices and long-term cost-effectiveness. It calls for carefully designed observational studies of community screening and more evidence on screening frequency and outcomes for high-risk children.

blocks.title: Tools for screening for TB
blocks.content:
5.2.1 Computer-aided detection
Further evidence is needed about the performance of CAD software stratified according to the 
characteristics of the individual being evaluated (e.g. by smear status, HIV status, age cohort, history 
of TB, smoking status, sex) to allow for better setting-specific and patient-specific calibration of 
CAD programmes.
More research on users’ perspectives is needed about CAD technologies in TB screening and triage, 
including their perceived acceptability to patients, providers and other stakeholders.
The development and evaluation of CAD programmes for automated de

summary.text: Lists research gaps on screening tools, including CAD performance across patient groups, user acceptability and CAD for children. It also calls for studies of higher C-reactive protein cut-offs in people with HIV and of complete screening and diagnostic algorithms against patient outcomes.

blocks.title: Operational research

summary.text: Suggests operational research topics for TB screening programmes, such as algorithm performance, acceptability, cost-effectiveness and local CAD calibration, and calls for larger randomized trials.
